For models, the practical response is to treat a report as a hypothesis and test it by eliciting the behavior independently. The evaluation is a confusion matrix of report versus behavior, not a transcript of an interview.

The official write-up, per the notes, reports false positives on models without specifically trained behaviors. A plausible mechanism: every training example involved a model with some behavior to describe, so the adapter may have learned a prior that there is always something to find, and a benign fine-tune that merely shifts weights can look like an anomaly. The fix is empirical rather than assumed: evaluate on unchanged bases and harmless fine-tunes, report the false-positive rate at fixed settings, and consider including such null models as negative examples in any future training. Without negatives, a tool can score well on positives while being unusable for screening.

A fingerprint is any feature of how a model was trained that correlates with its behavior in the training set without being the behavior itself. If each behavior in the training data was implanted with one recipe, behavior and recipe are collinear: observational data cannot reveal which one the adapter uses. This is an identifiability problem, solved by intervention. Create models with the same behavior from different recipes, and with the same recipe but different behaviors, then see which variable predicts the report. This is the logic of a factorial experiment, and it tells you what the tool depends on, not just whether it works.

Calibration means that among reports given with confidence c, a fraction c are correct, which can be examined with reliability diagrams and expected calibration error. Allowing 'uncertain' creates selective prediction: coverage is the fraction answered, and precision among answered often rises as coverage falls, tracing a risk-coverage curve. Confidence for text reports may come from token log-probabilities, agreement across several sampled reports, or a separate verifier. The trade-off is explicit: abstentions leave cases unresolved and require some other audit method. How best to derive usable confidence from free-text introspection is an open problem.

Once a tool is used for auditing, someone may optimize against it, as with any fixed detector; adversarial examples and obfuscated-activation attacks on latent monitors are well-known analogues. A pre-attack score measures performance on a non-adaptive distribution, so it cannot support a claim about robustness. Project 8 proposes training models against the adapter, then evaluating new held-out models and measuring behavior independently, to learn whether failures are specific to one attacker or general. The assumption to adopt in security-style reasoning is that the attacker knows the tool, since secrecy of a detector is a fragile defense.

Reliability is a bundle of properties: sensitivity, specificity, coverage, robustness to distribution shift, and robustness to adaptation. To decide whether a report deserves trust, combine them with prevalence: PPV = TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1-π)). With purely illustrative numbers TPR = 0.8, FPR = 0.1 and prevalence 5 percent, PPV is about 0.30, so most positive reports would be false alarms despite seemingly good rates. That is why one correct report on one model is insufficient evidence, and why the useful question is when the report deserves trust, not whether the tool works.
fellowship-10-introspection-foundation-0.further: Common misconceptions: that a confession is evidence by itself, that good performance on average means each report is dependable, and that a tool can be certified once. Open problems include building null models into training, obtaining calibrated confidence, defining what 'coverage' means for behaviors nobody planted, and measuring robustness against attackers who control the weights. These questions are taken up in the project 8 book. The wider lesson, shared with the detector books in this collection, is to assess an audit tool as a measurement instrument: with false-alarm rates, shift robustness and adversarial tests, not with a few impressive examples.

panels: Git is a content-addressable object store with a thin naming layer on top. Four object types live in .git/objects: a blob holds file bytes, a tree maps names and modes to blob or tree ids, a commit points to one tree plus zero or more parent commits with author, committer and message, and an annotated tag points to another object. An object's id is the hash (SHA-1 by default, SHA-256 optionally) of a header 'type size' plus its content, so identical content is stored once. A commit is a full snapshot of the tree, not a diff; delta compression happens later in packfiles. History is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of commits, and the 'staging area' is a file, .git/index.

git init creates the .git directory: objects/, refs/, a HEAD file (normally the text 'ref: refs/heads/main'), and config. git clone is a macro: init, add a remote called origin with a fetch refspec such as +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*, fetch all objects, create a local branch from the remote's default, and record branch.<name>.remote and .merge so pull and push know their upstream. 'origin' is only a conventional name. git remote -v reads URLs from .git/config; fetch and push URLs can differ, for instance with pushurl, which is why both lines are printed.

The index is a sorted list of entries: path, file mode, blob id, a stage number (0 normally, 1 to 3 during conflicts) and cached stat data used to detect changes quickly. git add hashes the file's current contents, writes a blob into the object store, and updates the entry, so what is staged is a snapshot at the moment of add; later edits show as unstaged again. git status is two comparisons: HEAD against the index (to be committed), and the index against the working tree (not staged). Untracked means no index entry. git restore --staged copies the HEAD version of the path back into the index; it never touches your working file.

git commit runs three steps: write the index out as a tree object, create a commit object with that tree and the current HEAD as parent, and move the current branch ref to the new commit. --amend does not edit anything: it creates a new commit with the old commit's parents and a new tree or message, then moves the branch ref. Because a commit id covers its tree, parents, author and message, any change produces a different id, and all descendants would need new ids as well. The old commit becomes unreachable but stays in the object store and reflog (30 to 90 days by default), which is why amending already-pushed commits causes divergence.

A branch is a ref: a file under .git/refs/heads containing one commit id (or a line in packed-refs). Creating one is writing 41 bytes. HEAD normally holds a symbolic ref to the current branch, so committing moves that branch; a detached HEAD holds a commit id directly, and commits made there are not on any branch. git switch updates HEAD, the index and the working tree to the target commit's tree, refusing if that would overwrite local changes. git merge first finds the merge base. If the current commit is an ancestor of the target, it fast-forwards (just moves the ref). Otherwise it does a three-way merge and records a commit with two parents.

git fetch downloads missing objects and updates remote-tracking refs such as refs/remotes/origin/main; it never changes your local branches or files. git pull is fetch followed by merge of the upstream (or rebase if configured). git push uploads objects and asks the server to move a ref; the server refuses non-fast-forward updates, meaning the remote tip must be an ancestor of what you push. -u stores the upstream in config. Remote-tracking refs are a cached view that can be stale until your next fetch. After rewriting history, prefer --force-with-lease, which refuses if the remote ref no longer matches what you last fetched, over plain --force.

git log walks the DAG, starting from the given commits or refs and following parent pointers; --all starts from every ref, --graph draws the topology, and decorations such as (HEAD -> main, origin/main) are the refs that point at each commit. git diff compares the index with the working tree; --staged compares HEAD with the index; diff HEAD compares both against the working tree. Diffs are computed on demand, not stored (the default algorithm is Myers; --patience and --histogram sometimes give clearer output). git show prints a commit's message and its diff against its parent (a combined diff for merges). Notation: HEAD~1 is the first parent, HEAD^2 the second parent of a merge, A..B means commits in B not in A.

Three mechanisms differ in what they touch. git restore <file> overwrites the working file from the index; uncommitted edits are lost and not in the reflog, though a file that had been git add-ed leaves a dangling blob that git fsck --lost-found might find. git revert creates a new commit applying the inverse patch, so history is preserved (reverting a merge needs -m to choose the mainline parent). git reset moves the current branch ref: --soft changes only the ref, --mixed also resets the index, --hard also overwrites the working tree. The panel's warning is correct for uncommitted work. Committed work discarded by reset --hard is usually recoverable: git reflog, then git reset --hard HEAD@{1} or ORIG_HEAD.

git stash records your work as commits: one for the index state and one for the working tree whose parents are the base commit and the index commit, stored under refs/stash with its reflog serving as the stack. By default untracked files are not included (-u adds them, -a adds ignored ones too). pop applies and drops, but if applying conflicts the stash is kept. A lightweight tag is just a ref in refs/tags; an annotated tag (-a) is an object with tagger, date and message, and is what git describe prefers. .gitignore affects only untracked files: a file already tracked stays tracked until git rm --cached, and patterns can also live in .git/info/exclude or a global excludes file.
swe-git-01.further: Common misconceptions: that Git stores diffs between versions (it stores snapshots and compresses them later), that branches are copies of files (they are movable pointers), and that git reset --hard is always unrecoverable (only uncommitted changes are). Open ideas to explore next: packfiles and garbage collection, how rebase and cherry-pick create new commit objects, and what the reflog protects. A useful habit is to draw the DAG and mark where HEAD, your branch and the remote-tracking branch point before and after any command; most surprises become obvious once you see which ref moved and which objects were left behind.

panels: Git reads configuration from layered files and later ones override earlier ones: system, global (~/.gitconfig), repository (.git/config) and optionally per-worktree; git config --list --show-origin prints each value with its source. user.name and user.email are copied into the author and committer fields of every commit you make; Git does not verify them, so anyone can claim any identity. Authentication of commits comes from signing (GPG or SSH signatures) and from the hosting service. Changing the settings later does not alter existing commits, whose identities are part of their hash. init.defaultBranch only affects the name chosen by future git init commands.

A remote is a name, a URL and refspecs, which describe how remote refs map to local remote-tracking refs. Any repository can serve as a remote; hosting services are just convenient ones, and servers normally keep bare repositories (object store and refs, no working tree). Clone options change what is transferred: --depth gives a shallow history, --filter=blob:none makes a partial clone that fetches file contents lazily, and --recurse-submodules initializes submodules. Git speaks https, ssh, git and file transports. Because every clone has the full object store by default, it is a complete backup of history, which is why Git is described as distributed.

The daily loop maps onto plumbing commands. add is hash-object -w plus update-index; commit is write-tree, commit-tree and update-ref. git push origin <branch> is shorthand for pushing refs/heads/<branch> to the remote's same-named ref, and is rejected if the remote has commits you lack. Small commits are not only tidy: they make git bisect, which binary-searches history for the commit that introduced a bug, effective, and they make revert and cherry-pick precise. git add -p stages individual hunks, letting one working tree become several logical commits. Hooks in .git/hooks, such as pre-commit, can run checks before the commit object is created.

The log is a traversal of the DAG, and options select or format the walk: --stat and -p show changes, -S<text> finds commits that changed the count of a string (the pickaxe), --follow tracks a file across renames, and A..B lists commits reachable from B but not from A. git show <branch> shows the tip commit; git show <rev>:<path> prints a file as it existed in that revision. git blame annotates each line with the commit that last changed it. Pagers like less are a display convenience, not part of Git's semantics. Many history queries are reachability questions, so knowing which commits a ref reaches explains the output.

Branches are cheap because they are 41-byte ref files. checkout is overloaded, both switching branches and restoring files, which is why Git 2.23 added switch and restore with narrower roles. git branch -d refuses to delete a branch whose commits are not merged into its upstream or HEAD, a reachability check, while -D forces. Deleting a branch deletes only the ref; commits remain until garbage collection if nothing else reaches them, and the reflog may still list them. branch -m renames the ref, its reflog and related config. Commits made on a detached HEAD are unnamed and can be lost, so create a branch before leaving.

Use the safest tool that does the job. reset moves the branch ref: --soft keeps index and files, --mixed (the default) resets the index, --hard resets files too. The reflog is the recovery net: it logs every movement of HEAD and each branch in .git/logs, addressable as HEAD@{n} or main@{yesterday}, and ORIG_HEAD records where HEAD was before a risky operation such as reset, merge or rebase. After a mistake, git reflog then git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD or HEAD@{n} often restores committed work. Limits: the reflog is local, entries expire (by default after 90 days if reachable and 30 if not), and uncommitted changes never enter it.

Remote-tracking branches such as origin/main are local, read-only bookmarks of where the remote's branch was at your last fetch; they are not live. fetch --prune also deletes bookmarks for branches removed upstream. pull is fetch plus merging the upstream into the current branch; git pull --ff-only fails instead of creating a surprise merge commit, and pull.rebase changes the second step to a rebase. Push is rejected unless it is a fast-forward of the remote ref; --force-with-lease turns a forced push into a conditional one, verifying the remote still matches your tracking ref. git remote remove deletes the remote's configuration and its tracking refs, but not your local branches.

A stash entry is a commit (a merge commit, in fact, with the base commit and an index snapshot as parents, plus a third parent holding untracked files when -u is used), referenced from refs/stash; earlier entries are in that ref's reflog, which is why stash@{2} works. apply re-applies the stash with a three-way merge, so it can succeed on a different base or conflict; pop does apply then drop only if apply succeeded. A dropped stash is not instantly gone: its commit becomes unreachable and can often be found by git fsck --unreachable until garbage collection. git stash branch <name> creates a branch from the stash's base commit and applies it there, avoiding conflicts.

Cherry-pick re-applies a change, not a commit. Git takes the difference between the picked commit and its parent and applies it onto HEAD as a three-way merge, using the picked commit's parent as base. The result is a new commit with a different id because its parent and committer data differ, although the author and message are copied; -x appends a note recording the source. Duplicates are the downside: later merging both lines may conflict or silently dedupe depending on context. Picking a merge commit requires -m to say which parent is the mainline. In-progress state lives in the repository (CHERRY_PICK_HEAD and a sequencer directory), which is what --continue and --abort use.

Merge adds a commit with two parents, so the DAG records that two lines of work joined and nothing is rewritten. Rebase finds the commits reachable from your branch but not from the target, detaches HEAD at the target tip, applies each commit as if by cherry-pick, and finally moves your branch ref to the result. The originals are not changed, just orphaned (reachable via reflog and ORIG_HEAD). Because the rebased commits have new ids, anyone who built on the old ones now has duplicates and a diverged history, hence the rule about shared commits. After rebasing a branch you already pushed, use --force-with-lease. By default, rebase flattens merge commits unless --rebase-merges is used.

A lightweight tag is a ref to a commit; an annotated tag (-a) is an object storing tagger, date, message and optionally a signature, and tools such as git describe use annotated tags by default. Tags do not move on their own, and a tag that is already published should not be moved, since clients do not update existing tags on ordinary fetch. Tags are not pushed by default: push a named tag, use --follow-tags for annotated tags reachable from pushed commits, or --tags for all. Removing a remote tag is git push origin --delete <tag> (or the refspec :refs/tags/<tag>), separately from git tag -d, which only deletes your local copy.

A submodule is a pointer: the parent repository's tree contains a special entry (mode 160000, a 'gitlink') naming an exact commit in another repository, while .gitmodules records the path and URL. The parent tracks a commit, not a branch, so git submodule update checks out that recorded commit as a detached HEAD in the submodule. --remote moves the submodule to its configured branch tip, after which the parent shows a modified pointer you must commit. A common pitfall is committing the new pointer without pushing the submodule's commit first, which leaves collaborators unable to fetch it. Clone with --recurse-submodules or initialize afterwards.

An alias is a config entry under [alias] that Git expands before dispatching the command; one that begins with ! runs as a shell command, so it can chain several operations. Aliases cannot shadow built-in commands. The log alias lg expands to the options listed, so lg --stat appends further options as you would for the full command. Config layering applies, so a global alias is available everywhere unless a repository overrides it. A caution: aliases like co for checkout hide which verb is running and keep the older overloaded command in muscle memory; it is worth knowing the expansion and, for restoring or switching, the newer switch and restore commands.
swe-git-02.further: Common misconceptions: that pull is a safe read-only operation (it merges into your branch), that rebase 'moves' commits (it creates copies), that deleting a branch deletes its commits, and that a remote-tracking branch shows the server's current state. Next steps: learn git reflog until recovery feels routine, read about packfiles and garbage collection to see when unreachable objects vanish, and practice interactive rebase on a throwaway branch. A reliable safety habit is to create a backup branch or note the current commit id before any operation that rewrites history, because a named ref makes recovery trivial.
